nodes.title: Updates
nodes.body:
January 2, 1990.  T. Czapla; NOAA SEA Division

FLELMR CODE:  1733

Scientific Name: Micropogonias undulates
Common Name: Atlantic Croaker
Other Common Names: Croaker; crocus; hardhead; king billy; la corbina (793).

nodes.title: Classification
nodes.body:
Phylum:	Chordata
	Class:   	Osteichthyes
	Order:		Perciformes
	Family:	Sciaenidae

nodes.title: Value
nodes.body:
Commercial:  Over 10 million pounds estimated at $4.6 million croaker were taken by commercial fishermen in the United States; 9.5 million pounds were caught within 3 miles of the coast (513).  Major methods of harvest include pound nets, haul seines, otter trawls, and gill nets with some additional catches made by trammel and fyke nets (462).

Recreational:  United States marine recreational catch was over 6.6 million pounds in 1988 for the Gulf coast, the majority being caught inland (513).

Indicator:  This species is a bottom feeder which often accumulates contaminants and is a target species for the National Status and Trends Program.  The effects of sub-lethal copper exposure (626) and lead on glutathione levels (371) have also been studied.

nodes.title: Geographic Range
nodes.body:
Overall:  Atlantic croaker occurs in coastal waters of the western Atlantic from Cape Cod, Massachusetts to Campeche Bank, Mexico.

Within Study Area:  Atlantic croaker is considered the most common estuarine fish in the northern Gulf of Mexico.  Common throughout the Indian River Lagoon (887 1195 1196 997 1242).

Migrations and Movements:
The adults have seasonal inshore and offshore migrations although some appear to remain in offshore waters (30 - 50 fa) year round (553).  Adults move up bays and estuaries in spring, randomly in summer and ocean-ward and southerly in fall.  Larvae are carried by longshore currents into nearshore areas where tidal flow transports them into estuarine areas (150).  Larval recruitment into estuaries occurs from October to May peaking between November and February (751 431).  As they mature into juveniles they move up into headwater areas.  After spending 6 - 8 months in the estuary, offshore emigration begins in late March or early April at ca. 50 mm SL or larger and continues until November (374 553 751 778 604 431).  Emigration cues are probably governed more by fluctuations in environmental conditions in the nursery area (e.g. tides, temperature, salinity, day length, etc.) and not just by size (122 778).

nodes.title: Life Mode
nodes.body:
Eggs and Larva: Eggs and early larvae are pelagic and planktonic.  Early larvae are found on the mid- to outer continental shelf but become generally uniform throughout the shelf.  Later stages become more demersal and occur in more inshore to estuarine areas.
Juveniles become still more demersal and move into tidal creeks.
Adults are demersal and move between estuarine and oceanic waters (793 149 150).

nodes.title: BENTHIC HABITAT
nodes.body:
Habitat Type:  Adults are estuarine to oceanic and have been collected from 1 - 90 m; juveniles are estuarine to riverine; larvae are oceanic to estuarine and early larvae and eggs are marine.  Cowan (149) and Cowan and Shaw (150) collected recently spawned larvae at depths ranging from 15 to 115 m or from about 20 to 200 km from shore.  Most small larvae were collected near midshelf about 65 - 125 km from shore.  Fish three years old tend to dominate estuaries in North Carolina while those >3 years old are found mostly offshore (610).

Substrate:  Practically all sizes of croaker beyond the planktonic stage are associated with soft bottoms (793). Juveniles occur over mud-sand in shallow estuarine and tidal creek areas, i.e., fine unconsolidated substrates.  Adults are associated with mud-sand, oyster reefs, shell and live bottoms in deeper waters.

nodes.title: Physical/Chemical Characteristics
nodes.body:
Salinity:  Atlantic croaker are euryhaline, having been collected at 0 - 40 ppt and rarely at 75 ppt (651 793).  Juvenile croaker utilize low salinity and oligohaline areas, being most abundant at <15 ppt, and are more tolerant of low salinities than adults.  Adults are found in polyhaline to euhaline areas.  Eggs and larvae are found in euhaline areas.  Larvae have been found in salinities ranging from 22 to 36 ppt (751 604 149 150).

Temperature:  Croaker have been collected from 0.4 - 35.5 C in the Gulf of Mexico.  Juveniles appear to be more cold tolerant (6 - 20 C) than adults.  Adults are rarely found below 10 C.  Eggs and newly hatched larvae are found at 18 – 25 C with larger and older larvae found at progressively decreasing temperatures.   Larvae have been found in temperatures as low as 10 C (470 751 561 149 150).

Oxygen:  Dissolved oxygen requirements are unknown, but the presence of this species in poorly oxygenated canals indicates a tolerance for low D.O. (793).  Captures at DO concentrations from 1 through 13 ppm have been reported with most occurring between 8 and 13 ppm (431).

nodes.title: Reproduction
nodes.body:
Mode: Sexual, separate sexes, oviparous with external fertilization.

Mating and Spawning:  Croaker have a prolonged fall to late-spring spawning season (374 763 648).  Spawning occurs from September through May, with a peak in October, specifically calculated around mid-October, and possibly November (614 763 9 431).  Probably takes place in open Gulf near island passes (614 793).

Reproductive Capacity:  Sheridan et al. (648) found fecundities ranged from 27,000 for 136 mm SL to 1,075,000 for a 318 mm SL specimen.  Mercer (462) cited a study that reported a fecundity range of 100,800 to 1,742,000 for fish 196 to 390 mm TL.

Growth and Development
Egg:  Indirect and external; egg size range 0.70 - 0.80 mm.

Larval/Juvenile:  Larvae hatch at 1.3 - 2.0 mm.  Hatching time is 29 - 32 h at 23 C and 26 - 30 h at 25 C.  In Texas, young of the year appear in November to January at 10 - 50 mm TL.  Juveniles range in size from 11 to 140 mm TL (363 763).  One study estimates juvenile growth rate at 0.47 mm/day or 14.2 mm/mo (23), while another estimates it as 3.1 mm/wk (758).

Adults:  Maturity was reached after the first year’s growth to 140 - 170 mm TL (763).  Most adults live up to 3 years with some living 4 to 5 years, but rarely greater (202 793).  In North Carolina, fish older than 3 years were found offshore, but were rare in estuaries (610).  The oldest fish recovered there were estimated to be 7 years old.  Predicted TL for year classes are: 176.6 mm for age 1; 261.5 mm at age 2; 331.0 mm at age 3; 388.0 mm at age 4; 434.5 mm  at age 5; and 472.7 mm at age 6 (610).  Largest recorded specimen is 668 mm TL (601).

nodes.title: Eating
nodes.body:
Young of the year fish consumed primarily polychaete worms, while older fish principally fed on crustaceans (stomatopods, shrimps and crabs) and fish (648 462).  Adults are opportunistic bottom feeding carnivores.  Early juveniles (15_30 mm) feed on zooplankton, switching to benthic mode as they become older and begin consuming infaunal and epifaunal organisms sorted from bottom debris.  Feeding is by sight, olfaction, and touch (462).

Ecological Interactions and Notes
White and Chittenden (763) show some habitat segregation by life stage, with smaller (<200 mm TL), younger individuals (age 0) occupying the bays and muddy bottoms, while the larger (>200 mm TL), older individuals (age I+) are more localized around oyster reefs.

Predation:  Predators of Atlantic croaker are larger piscivorous species such as striped bass, southern flounder, bull shark, blue catfish, yellow bass, spotted seatrout, croaker, sheepshead, blue fish, and weakfish (462).

nodes.title: Growth
nodes.body:
The Bertalanffy growth model for Atlantic croaker is:

 	TLt = 645(1 _ e_0.20(t + 0.60))
      For t = age in years (610).

sections.heading: Updates
sections.content:
January 2, 1990.  T. Czapla; NOAA SEA Division

FLELMR CODE:  1733

Scientific Name: Micropogonias undulates
Common Name: Atlantic Croaker
Other Common Names: Croaker; crocus; hardhead; king billy; la corbina (793).

sections.heading: Classification
sections.content:
Phylum:	Chordata
	Class:   	Osteichthyes
	Order:		Perciformes
	Family:	Sciaenidae

sections.heading: Value
sections.content:
Commercial:  Over 10 million pounds estimated at $4.6 million croaker were taken by commercial fishermen in the United States; 9.5 million pounds were caught within 3 miles of the coast (513).  Major methods of harvest include pound nets, haul seines, otter trawls, and gill nets with some additional catches made by trammel and fyke nets (462).

Recreational:  United States marine recreational catch was over 6.6 million pounds in 1988 for the Gulf coast, the majority being caught inland (513).

Indicator:  This species is a bottom feeder which often accumulates contaminants and is a target species for the National Status and Trends Program.  The effects of sub-lethal copper exposure (626) and lead on glutathione levels (371) have also been studied.

sections.heading: Geographic Range
sections.content:
Overall:  Atlantic croaker occurs in coastal waters of the western Atlantic from Cape Cod, Massachusetts to Campeche Bank, Mexico.

Within Study Area:  Atlantic croaker is considered the most common estuarine fish in the northern Gulf of Mexico.  Common throughout the Indian River Lagoon (887 1195 1196 997 1242).

Migrations and Movements:
The adults have seasonal inshore and offshore migrations although some appear to remain in offshore waters (30 - 50 fa) year round (553).  Adults move up bays and estuaries in spring, randomly in summer and ocean-ward and southerly in fall.  Larvae are carried by longshore currents into nearshore areas where tidal flow transports them into estuarine areas (150).  Larval recruitment into estuaries occurs from October to May peaking between November and February (751 431).  As they mature into juveniles they move up into headwater areas.  After spending 6 - 8 months in the estuary, offshore emigration begins in late March or early April at ca. 50 mm SL or larger and continues until November (374 553 751 778 604 431).  Emigration cues are probably governed more by fluctuations in environmental conditions in the nursery area (e.g. tides, temperature, salinity, day length, etc.) and not just by size (122 778).

sections.heading: Life Mode
sections.content:
Eggs and Larva: Eggs and early larvae are pelagic and planktonic.  Early larvae are found on the mid- to outer continental shelf but become generally uniform throughout the shelf.  Later stages become more demersal and occur in more inshore to estuarine areas.
Juveniles become still more demersal and move into tidal creeks.
Adults are demersal and move between estuarine and oceanic waters (793 149 150).

sections.heading: BENTHIC HABITAT
sections.content:
Habitat Type:  Adults are estuarine to oceanic and have been collected from 1 - 90 m; juveniles are estuarine to riverine; larvae are oceanic to estuarine and early larvae and eggs are marine.  Cowan (149) and Cowan and Shaw (150) collected recently spawned larvae at depths ranging from 15 to 115 m or from about 20 to 200 km from shore.  Most small larvae were collected near midshelf about 65 - 125 km from shore.  Fish three years old tend to dominate estuaries in North Carolina while those >3 years old are found mostly offshore (610).

Substrate:  Practically all sizes of croaker beyond the planktonic stage are associated with soft bottoms (793). Juveniles occur over mud-sand in shallow estuarine and tidal creek areas, i.e., fine unconsolidated substrates.  Adults are associated with mud-sand, oyster reefs, shell and live bottoms in deeper waters.

sections.heading: Physical/Chemical Characteristics
sections.content:
Salinity:  Atlantic croaker are euryhaline, having been collected at 0 - 40 ppt and rarely at 75 ppt (651 793).  Juvenile croaker utilize low salinity and oligohaline areas, being most abundant at <15 ppt, and are more tolerant of low salinities than adults.  Adults are found in polyhaline to euhaline areas.  Eggs and larvae are found in euhaline areas.  Larvae have been found in salinities ranging from 22 to 36 ppt (751 604 149 150).

Temperature:  Croaker have been collected from 0.4 - 35.5 C in the Gulf of Mexico.  Juveniles appear to be more cold tolerant (6 - 20 C) than adults.  Adults are rarely found below 10 C.  Eggs and newly hatched larvae are found at 18 – 25 C with larger and older larvae found at progressively decreasing temperatures.   Larvae have been found in temperatures as low as 10 C (470 751 561 149 150).

Oxygen:  Dissolved oxygen requirements are unknown, but the presence of this species in poorly oxygenated canals indicates a tolerance for low D.O. (793).  Captures at DO concentrations from 1 through 13 ppm have been reported with most occurring between 8 and 13 ppm (431).

sections.heading: Reproduction
sections.content:
Mode: Sexual, separate sexes, oviparous with external fertilization.

Mating and Spawning:  Croaker have a prolonged fall to late-spring spawning season (374 763 648).  Spawning occurs from September through May, with a peak in October, specifically calculated around mid-October, and possibly November (614 763 9 431).  Probably takes place in open Gulf near island passes (614 793).

Reproductive Capacity:  Sheridan et al. (648) found fecundities ranged from 27,000 for 136 mm SL to 1,075,000 for a 318 mm SL specimen.  Mercer (462) cited a study that reported a fecundity range of 100,800 to 1,742,000 for fish 196 to 390 mm TL.

Growth and Development
Egg:  Indirect and external; egg size range 0.70 - 0.80 mm.

Larval/Juvenile:  Larvae hatch at 1.3 - 2.0 mm.  Hatching time is 29 - 32 h at 23 C and 26 - 30 h at 25 C.  In Texas, young of the year appear in November to January at 10 - 50 mm TL.  Juveniles range in size from 11 to 140 mm TL (363 763).  One study estimates juvenile growth rate at 0.47 mm/day or 14.2 mm/mo (23), while another estimates it as 3.1 mm/wk (758).

Adults:  Maturity was reached after the first year’s growth to 140 - 170 mm TL (763).  Most adults live up to 3 years with some living 4 to 5 years, but rarely greater (202 793).  In North Carolina, fish older than 3 years were found offshore, but were rare in estuaries (610).  The oldest fish recovered there were estimated to be 7 years old.  Predicted TL for year classes are: 176.6 mm for age 1; 261.5 mm at age 2; 331.0 mm at age 3; 388.0 mm at age 4; 434.5 mm  at age 5; and 472.7 mm at age 6 (610).  Largest recorded specimen is 668 mm TL (601).

sections.heading: Eating
sections.content:
Young of the year fish consumed primarily polychaete worms, while older fish principally fed on crustaceans (stomatopods, shrimps and crabs) and fish (648 462).  Adults are opportunistic bottom feeding carnivores.  Early juveniles (15_30 mm) feed on zooplankton, switching to benthic mode as they become older and begin consuming infaunal and epifaunal organisms sorted from bottom debris.  Feeding is by sight, olfaction, and touch (462).

Ecological Interactions and Notes
White and Chittenden (763) show some habitat segregation by life stage, with smaller (<200 mm TL), younger individuals (age 0) occupying the bays and muddy bottoms, while the larger (>200 mm TL), older individuals (age I+) are more localized around oyster reefs.

Predation:  Predators of Atlantic croaker are larger piscivorous species such as striped bass, southern flounder, bull shark, blue catfish, yellow bass, spotted seatrout, croaker, sheepshead, blue fish, and weakfish (462).

sections.content:
The Bertalanffy growth model for Atlantic croaker is:

 	TLt = 645(1 _ e_0.20(t + 0.60))
      For t = age in years (610).
